title: Genotype-guided dosing for patients A to D

segs.text: Section six. Genotype-guided dosing. When a metabolizing enzyme clears a drug, the patient's genotype for that enzyme predicts how fast the drug is removed, and that rate is a phenotype. Give everyone the same dose and exposures differ widely; adjust each dose to the genotype and exposure is the same. She said, the goal of pharmacogenomics is to ensure efficacy and prevent toxicity.

The figure follows four patients, first on the same dose for everyone, one hundred percent of average, then on genotype-based doses. Patient A has both alleles non-functional, no working sip two D six: a standard dose cannot be cleared, the concentration goes too high, and a lower than average dose prevents toxicity. Patient D has extra copies of the gene: a standard dose is metabolized away, the A U C, area under the curve, is very low and never therapeutic, and a much higher dose ensures efficacy.

Patient B has one non-functional allele and gets a dose slightly below average. Patient C has two functional alleles and gets a dose above average. All four end with the same therapeutic A U C, because each dose matches that genotype's metabolizing capability.

An earlier figure shows the same principle with warfarin. S warfarin unbound clearance falls step by step across sip two C nine genotypes, from star one, star one at the top, through genotypes carrying star two or star three, to star three, star three, the lowest, because star two and star three have decreased activity.

In the Pharm G K B information flow, genes act on pharmacokinetics, meaning absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion, or on pharmacodynamics, meaning the target, mechanism and response. Either way the clinical outcome is efficacy or toxicity.
